verdict: redesign (the turn record), adjust (the front door machinery). Split inbound_message. It does two different jobs: an async WhatsApp chat message (dedupe, queue, typing/interim/failure/reply markers) and a committed, channel-neutral turn (the batch an undo reaches, its record, its question, its undo mark). MCP needs only the second job, yet today it has to fake the first: wamid 'mcp:<id>', kind 'tool', status 'done', payload as result store, the account's wa_id (src/mcp/write.ts:117-127). Batch identity is also keyed on the WhatsApp wa_id rather than account_id (src/ledger.ts:188-190, `i.wa_id = a.wa_id`), so a third channel without a wa_id cannot make a batch at all. That is the strongest from-scratch argument, and the live DB is small enough that a migration can keep the ids and rewrite no effect rows. The claim, lane, sweep and send markers are close to minimal for at-most-once plus ordering on one replica, and I would keep them, but they have two ordering holes. Claims run in RETURNING order, not id order. A kick claims only the webhook's wamids, so an older pending row from the same sender can be overtaken. On the second half of the council question, I would not add a separate effect log now. The per-table pointer columns are what the live reads need, and an effect log beside them would be a second source of truth. Repointing those FKs to `turn` and taking one account-row lock gets most of the simplification.

keep.item: At-most-once send protocol on the WhatsApp row: send_started_at committed before the Graph call, stale started rows go to 'unknown', and only a 4xx that proves nothing was sent goes back to pending (src/store.ts:154-162, 354-360; src/process.ts:152-199)
keep.why: No library or Postgres feature provides this. It is a protocol, and it is already the minimal form: one marker column per outbound kind, checked by single-row predicates. A queue library would be at-least-once and would not remove it.

keep.item: Fencing every post-claim write with `id AND status='processing' AND attempts=<claimed>` (src/store.ts:116-117)
keep.why: It is a fencing token. It still matters on 'one replica' because a Railway deploy briefly runs the old and new process side by side (my guess; the code comment at src/process.ts:609-612 assumes the same). It costs one predicate.

keep.item: Interim, failure and reply markers as columns on the same row (interim_sent_at, failure_sent_at, send_started_at)
keep.why: Their mutual exclusion is enforced inside one row's UPDATE predicate (src/store.ts:306-307, 330-331). Moving them to a delivery table would need a parent-row lock to keep that exclusion, which is more machinery for the same guarantee.

keep.item: FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED claim with stale takeover after 120 s (src/store.ts:169-181, src/server.ts:22)
keep.why: This is the documented queue pattern. It guards against overlapping ticks and the deploy overlap.

keep.item: In-memory per-sender lane that passes its turn at the commit, not at the send (src/process.ts:534-556)
keep.why: The context read and the LLM call happen outside any transaction, so no database lock can order them without holding a connection through a call of several seconds. A promise chain is the simplest correct tool on one process. Passing the turn at the commit is the right cut (docs/spec.md:212).

keep.item: The commit point as one short transaction that takes the model output as input (src/store.ts:274-297)
keep.why: No LLM call runs inside sql.begin, the guard row is locked FOR UPDATE, and nothing awaits between the abort check and the commit (src/process.ts:406-458). Correct, and keep it.

keep.item: resolve.ts as pure code that owns short answers, bare undo, link codes and disconnect
keep.why: It keeps the model out of deciding what '2' or 'sí' means, which is a safety rule. It has no IO and is easy to test. Only the composition that calls it moves (see redesign).

keep.item: MCP idempotency semantics: same account, tool and input hash replays the first result, and a different call under the same id is refused (src/mcp/write.ts:162-181)
keep.why: It matches the Stripe/Brandur design. Only where the key is stored is wrong (see redesign).

keep.item: The `reply` table for outbound wamids and their delivery statuses, upserted in any arrival order (src/store.ts:134-146)
keep.why: It is small, correct and channel-specific. The FK to inbound_message stays valid after the split, because MCP never sends.

keep.item: Pointer columns (superseded_by, deleted_by, forgotten_by, cancelled_by, restores) as the source of truth, with no separate effect log yet (cross-group view)
keep.why: The live predicate reads these columns on every query, and reversal differs by entity: reminders recompute next_due_at (src/undo.ts:96-97). An effect log beside them would be a second truth that can disagree. Repointing them to `turn` removes the wa_id coupling at no cost. The undo group should decide whether an effect log replaces them.

keep.item: 30 s tick with no LISTEN/NOTIFY (src/server.ts:79-85)
keep.why: Webhooks kick work in-process, so NOTIFY would only help the deploy hand-off case below. A shorter tick fixes that case more cheaply.

redesign.item: Split inbound_message into a channel-neutral `turn` (the committed batch and its record) plus the existing WhatsApp row (chat message, queue and delivery)
redesign.problem: One row holds five jobs. Batch-ness is derived from 'action and reply_text set and undoes null' (src/ledger.ts:144-147). MCP fakes a chat message to get a batch id (src/mcp/write.ts:121-127), then settles it in a second step (settleBatchRow, src/ledger.ts:153-175). Batches are found by WhatsApp id, not account (src/ledger.ts:188-190), so MCP has to carry `waId` (src/mcp/write.ts:31-32), and a future channel without a wa_id cannot make one. Every chat-only query has to remember `channel = 'whatsapp'`, in seven places: store.ts:162, 168, 174, 234, 245, latency-report.ts:29 and reminders/send.ts:185. Forgetting the filter in reminders/send.ts:185 would let an MCP write open the 24 h window, and a free-form reminder would then be sent outside Meta's window.
redesign.proposal:
New table, inserted only inside a commit transaction, so every row is committed:
```sql
CREATE TABLE turn (
  id          bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
  account_id  bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES account(id),
  channel     text   NOT NULL CHECK (channel IN ('whatsapp','mcp')),
  action      text   NOT NULL,          -- label (actionLabel)
  calls       jsonb  NOT NULL,          -- what ran (today inbound_message.command)
  record      text   NOT NULL,          -- code-rendered reply/record (today reply_text)
  question    jsonb,                    -- see the question item
  undoes      bigint REFERENCES turn(id),
  created_at  timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  CONSTRAINT turn_undoes_other CHECK (undoes IS NULL OR undoes <> id),
  CONSTRAINT turn_question_chat CHECK (question IS NULL OR channel = 'whatsapp'));
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX turn_undoes_idx ON turn(undoes) WHERE undoes IS NOT NULL;
CREATE INDEX turn_account_idx ON turn(account_id, id DESC);
ALTER TABLE inbound_message ADD COLUMN turn_id bigint UNIQUE REFERENCES turn(id);
```
inbound_message stays the WhatsApp row and keeps wamid, wa_id, kind, body, payload, meta_ts, received_at, status, attempts, claimed_at, error, the four *_sent_at/send_started_at markers, timings, and the agent-run diagnostics (parsed, tool_calls, model_turns, model_ms). Those diagnostics stay there because a failed run has them and no turn (src/store.ts:327-328). It drops channel, action, reply_text, command, undoes, asked_numbers, asked_ids and pending.
Interfaces:
- `store.commit(c, m)`: lock account (next item), check `turn_id IS NULL AND failure_sent_at IS NULL` (replacing `reply_text IS NULL`, store.ts:278), `INSERT INTO turn … RETURNING id`, then `execute(tx, {turnId})`, then `UPDATE turn SET record, question`, then `UPDATE inbound_message SET turn_id, body/redaction, parsed, tool_calls, model_*`.
- `claimDue` returns `replyText` as `(SELECT record FROM turn WHERE id = turn_id)`.
- recordFailure and recordInterim test `turn_id IS NULL`.
- `conversation()` joins `inbound_message p JOIN turn t ON t.id = p.turn_id`. Same behaviour as today: the preceding chat row, of any status, still closes a question.
- `ApplyContext.batchId` (already a neutral name, src/apply.ts:51) becomes the turn id.
- ledger: `lastBatch` becomes `FROM turn i WHERE i.account_id = $1 AND i.id < $asking AND i.undoes IS NULL AND (EXISTS … same four probes on turn_id) AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM turn u WHERE u.undoes = i.id)`. Delete batchRow and settleBatchRow. settledBatches and markUndone move onto turn.
- undo.ts:104-107 reads `turn.channel`, or better takes `channel` as a parameter.
Migration 016_turn.sql, one transaction, ids preserved, so no effect row is rewritten:
1. `INSERT INTO turn (id, account_id, channel, action, calls, record, question, undoes, created_at) SELECT i.id, a.id, i.channel, i.action, COALESCE(i.command,'[]'), i.reply_text, <question built from the three columns>, i.undoes, i.received_at FROM inbound_message i JOIN account a ON a.wa_id = i.wa_id WHERE i.reply_text IS NOT NULL AND i.action IS NOT NULL ORDER BY i.id`. The self-FK is checked at statement end, and `undoes` always points to an earlier id.
2. `SELECT setval(pg_get_serial_sequence('turn','id'), GREATEST((SELECT max(id) FROM turn),1))`.
3. Run a DO block that RAISEs if any movement, fact or reminder inbound_message_id, deleted_by, forgotten_by or cancelled_by is not a turn id. This is the proof that nothing was orphaned.
4. `UPDATE inbound_message SET turn_id = id WHERE channel='whatsapp' AND id IN (SELECT id FROM turn)`.
5. Copy MCP rows into mcp_request (MCP item).
6. For movement(inbound_message_id, deleted_by), fact(inbound_message_id, forgotten_by) and reminder(inbound_message_id, cancelled_by): DROP the `…_fkey` constraint, ADD a FK to turn(id), and RENAME inbound_message_id to turn_id.
7. `DELETE FROM inbound_message WHERE channel='mcp'`. No `reply` rows point at these.
8. Drop the moved columns, `inbound_message_undoes_idx` and `channel`.
Take a Railway backup or pg_dump first, because the column drops are one-way. Build the migration and prove it on a copy of the live DB (about 100 rows).

redesign.item: Pending question: one `turn.question jsonb` instead of asked_numbers int[], asked_ids bigint[] and pending jsonb
redesign.problem: The question is stored as two parallel arrays plus a union. Zipping them falls back to id 0 when the lengths differ (src/store.ts:257-260). The forget_all and link kinds are special-cased three times: once in store (src/store.ts:252-254), again in process when building the model context (src/process.ts:363-371), and again in resolve (src/resolve.ts:70-79).
redesign.proposal: Store `question = {"options":[{"number":2,"id":417},…],"then":<Pending>|null}` on the turn that asked it, written in the same commit. Add `CHECK (question IS NULL OR jsonb_typeof(question->'options') = 'array')`. 'Answered' stays derived: the next chat row of the sender closes it, which is race-free under the lane. No new table and no close write. `conversation()` returns it as is (`PendingQuestion = {options, then}`), so store.ts:250-264 collapses to one line and process.ts:363-371 becomes a two-line projection. Keep it per chat conversation (`channel='whatsapp'` turns via the joined chat row), so an MCP write in between neither answers nor closes it, as today. It should not live on `account` (one mutable slot needs a clear-on-every-message write) or in memory (lost on restart, and a deploy is common).

redesign.item: One account-row lock at the start of every write transaction, in commit() and writeAsMcp
redesign.problem: Writes of one account from two channels are not serialized. The lane covers WhatsApp only (src/process.ts:535-556), and MCP writes bypass it. Mutual exclusion is spread across advisory namespaces (undo 7203002, src/undo.ts:86; facts 7203003; reminders 7203005) plus row locks taken in action order. The docs already record a known deadlock (docs/agent-spec.md:685-686, 1160). db.ts:19-20 lists only four of the five keys.
redesign.proposal: Make the first statement of `store.commit` and `writeAsMcp` `SELECT id FROM account WHERE id = ${accountId} FOR UPDATE`. One lock, a real row, held only for the short commit (no LLM inside). Every same-account write then runs strictly in order, whatever the channel. The lock-order hazard goes away (the guard row first, then the account, then movements; MCP takes the account, then movements). The undo, facts and reminders advisory locks become redundant and can be deleted by their groups. The commit also needs the account id before the transaction, which process.ts already has (src/process.ts:265). Add `lock_timeout` (for example 5 s) to the server pool's connection options, so a stuck lock fails the commit (and sends a notice) instead of hanging past Meta's patience.
redesign.evidence: src/undo.ts:86. src/db.ts:19-20. docs/agent-spec.md:685-686, 1160. src/mcp/write.ts:121 (no lane, no account lock). The README's postgres.js connection options have no default timeouts.
redesign.size: +4 in my group; -15 across facts, undo and reminders (cross-group)

redesign.item: MCP write recorded as a `turn` plus an `mcp_request` idempotency row, not as a fake inbound message
redesign.problem: The idempotency key is the global `wamid` UNIQUE ('mcp:'+request_id, src/mcp/write.ts:117). It is not scoped per account, so ownership has to be re-checked by hand at replay (`prior.wa_id !== r.waId`, src/mcp/write.ts:168). `payload` is reused as the result store (src/mcp/write.ts:150), and the synthetic one-entry audit and `model_turns = 0` (src/mcp/write.ts:134-144, ledger.ts:172) are noise.

redesign.size: +15 SQL, about -30 TS in write.ts and ledger.ts

redesign.item: Claim order: run claims in id order, and kick claims by sender, not by wamid
redesign.problem: (a) `UPDATE … WHERE id IN (SELECT … ORDER BY id … FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED) RETURNING` gives no guaranteed row order. The outer scan order (physical or hash order) decides it, and rows that were updated before, such as ones released on shutdown, sit elsewhere physically. kick queues lanes in array order (`claims.map(run)`, src/process.ts:573), and so does sweep (src/process.ts:585). A multi-message webhook or a post-restart sweep can therefore run one sender's messages out of order, so 'uy, era 3800' corrects the wrong row. The burst test posts one webhook per message (src/concurrency.test.ts:339-347), so it never exercises this. (b) kick claims only the webhook's own wamids (src/process.ts:572, store.ts:153). An older pending row from the same sender (released on shutdown at process.ts:412 or 524, or left by a failed insert batch at app.ts:94-97) is not in the lane, so the new message runs first. The old one waits up to 30 s for the tick and then usually fails its 30 s deadline with a notice.
redesign.proposal: (a) In claimDue, `WITH c AS (UPDATE … RETURNING …) SELECT * FROM c ORDER BY id`, or `rows.sort((x,y)=>x.id-y.id)`. One line. (b) `kick(senders: string[])` claims every due row of those wa_ids (`AND wa_id = ANY(${senders})`, limit 50), so older rows join the lane first, in id order. app.ts passes `messages.map(m => m.from)`. Add a test that inserts two pending rows and kicks the later one: the earlier one must reply first.
redesign.evidence: src/store.ts:169-183. src/process.ts:568-576, 584-585. src/app.ts:66-101. PG docs leave UPDATE…RETURNING order unspecified (my reading; I did not run EXPLAIN).
redesign.confidence: (a) medium-high (the order is not guaranteed; how often it goes wrong live is a guess); (b) high that the gap exists, low on frequency

redesign.item: Deploy hand-off: a row released by the old process waits up to 30 s
redesign.problem: On SIGTERM the old process puts its still-parsing rows back to pending (src/process.ts:410-414). The new process has already run its startup sweep (src/server.ts:84), so it finds them only at the next 30 s tick (src/server.ts:85). Measured from received_at, they then pass the 30 s deadline and get the failure notice (src/process.ts:510-515). That breaks 'never go silent / first signal under 1 s' on every deploy that lands mid-message. That Railway starts the new process before stopping the old one is my assumption.
redesign.proposal: Make the tick 5 s instead of 30 s. That is three indexed statements on an almost empty partial index every 5 s, the simplest fix. Alternatively, the releasing process runs `NOTIFY warren_due` and the server `sql.listen('warren_due', () => processor.sweep())`, with the tick kept as the safety net. I prefer the shorter tick.
redesign.evidence: src/process.ts:409-415, 520-527. src/server.ts:79-96. src/store.ts:22 (staleMs 120 s, unrelated: those rows are pending, not processing).
redesign.size: 1 line (tick) or +8 (NOTIFY)
redesign.confidence: medium (depends on Railway's deploy overlap, which I have not verified)

redesign.item: Move the 'answered by code' decision chain from process.ts into resolve.ts
redesign.problem: Policy about which short texts code answers sits in a nested ternary inside a 280-line closure (src/process.ts:332-341). That logic (link code first, a question's answer next, undo and disconnect only when no question is open, never for photos or voice) is pure and belongs beside the matchers it composes.
redesign.proposal: `export function codeAnswer(text, {kind, question, signIn}): Action | null` in resolve.ts, with unit tests for the precedence. process.ts calls it once. Also factor the duplicated normalize-and-strip in undoRequest and disconnectRequest (src/resolve.ts:122-125, 150-153) into one `words(text)` helper.
redesign.evidence: src/process.ts:327-344. src/resolve.ts:121-155.
redesign.size: ±0 net, +15 tests

redesign.item: Sweep runs its claims one after another across all senders
redesign.problem: `for (const c of claims) await run(c)` (src/process.ts:585) waits for each whole message, send included, before starting the next sender's. With a backlog after an outage, later senders' messages age past the 30 s deadline and get failure notices, although the lanes already order each sender.
redesign.proposal: Use `await Promise.all(claims.map(run))`, as kick does. The lanes keep per-sender order, and the pool (max 10) is not held during model calls.
redesign.evidence: src/process.ts:572-573 vs 584-586. Ageing at src/process.ts:509-515.

redesign.confidence: medium (irrelevant with one user, correct for more)

challenged_decisions.challenge: Not contradicted, but under-specified. Today it means per WhatsApp sender for context reads (the in-memory lane). Writes of one account from MCP and WhatsApp are not serialized against each other at all. Make it per account at the commit (account-row lock), and keep per chat sender for the parse. The lane also leaks in two places (RETURNING order, kick by wamid), so the guarantee holds only in the common path today.

Not contradicted as a goal, but the code misses it on a deploy hand-off. Rows released by the old process wait for the new process's next 30 s tick and usually end in the failure notice. A 5 s tick (or NOTIFY) closes this. The Railway overlap behaviour is my assumption.
Kept. Note only that the fencing (attempts guard, stale takeover) is still needed under it because of the deploy overlap. Do not simplify it away on the grounds of 'single replica'.

questions_for_owner: When a WhatsApp message fails (failure notice, no commit) between a '¿Cuál?' question and the answer '2', should the question still be answerable? Today the failed row closes it (src/store.ts:242-248 takes the latest chat row of any status). The redesign keeps that unless you say otherwise.
Should an MCP write in between close an open WhatsApp question? Today it does not, and the redesign keeps that. Its options are re-checked (owned and live) when used.
Is it acceptable for 016_turn.sql to be one-way (column drops), with a Railway backup taken just before? The alternative is a two-step migration that drops the columns one release later.
Railway deploy overlap: does the new container start and receive traffic before the old one gets SIGTERM? That decides whether the hand-off gap is real.
Should a no-op or refused MCP call with a request_id be recorded, so a retry replays the refusal? Today nothing is stored and a retry re-runs, which is safe. The redesign keeps that.

verdict: redesign, but only of the record, not of the queue. inbound_message does two kinds of job. Three of them share one lifecycle and one row lock and should stay together: the raw WhatsApp log, the claim state and the send markers. The other four are a different thing, the channel-neutral unit of committed work: batch identity for effects and undo, the stored reply and question, account ownership, and the MCP request record. Those should move to a new `turn` table, which docs/mcp-spec.md:30 and :120 already name as the planned overhaul. I would not add a channel delivery table now, because the mutual exclusion between a message's interim note, failure notice and reply is a single-row UPDATE today and a child table would make each of them a lock-then-insert. The claim, lane and marker machinery is close to minimal for at-most-once; what is wrong in it is that per-sender order lives in process memory and in the order rows are handed in, which I showed is not id order. Separately, one account-row lock at the two commit entry points would replace three advisory-lock namespaces and close a deadlock the docs still describe as impossible in one process.

keep.why: It is the smallest protocol that gives the owner's guarantee (src/process.ts:152-199, src/store.ts:355-359, :391-399). No queue library removes it: they are at-least-once.

keep.why: One fragment guards every post-claim write (src/store.ts:116-117). It is what makes a takeover safe during a Railway deploy, when two processes are alive at once.

keep.why: src/store.ts:274-297. A crash or replay cannot apply effects twice, and the failure notice and the commit exclude each other through the same row.

keep.why: src/mcp/write.ts:162-181 matches the Stripe design (key, request hash, stored response). Only where it is stored is wrong.

keep.why: src/process.ts:478. Ordering only needs the stored change; docs/spec.md:212 measured about 0.6 s saved per queued message.

keep.why: One upsert handles statuses in any arrival order, including a status that beats our own insert (src/store.ts:134-146).

redesign.item: Claim inside the per-sender lane, so order comes from the database
redesign.problem: Rows are claimed first and then chained 'in the order they were handed in' (src/process.ts:544-556, :572-573, :584-585). Three holes follow. (1) The claim's RETURNING order is not id order: on PGlite (PostgreSQL 18.6) the same statement returned 302,304,305,307,308,309,310,306,303,301, the heap order of a Hash Semi Join over a Seq Scan. In practice fresh rows sit in id order, so this bites only rows updated out of order. (2) Two webhooks from one sender each run three statements before their claim returns, so the later message can enter the lane first (reasoned, not reproduced). (3) Across a deploy the lane map is empty in the new process: message 1 is released to 'pending' at shutdown (src/process.ts:412) or stays 'processing' for 120 s, message 2 is kicked alone by wamid and answered first (reasoned, not reproduced). Also, a sweep claims up to 50 rows and works them one after another across all senders (:584-585), so claimed_at ages while rows wait and one sender's slow message delays another's toward its 30 s deadline.
redesign.proposal:
Keep the promise chain and the turn passing at commit. Move the claim into the lane step.

store.claimNext(waId): one UPDATE that takes the sender's oldest open row (`WHERE id = (SELECT id ... WHERE wa_id = $1 AND attempts < max AND (status = 'pending' OR stale) ORDER BY id LIMIT 1 FOR UPDATE)`), returning the Claim or null. Optional hardening: `AND NOT EXISTS` an older row of the sender that is 'processing', uncommitted and not stale (another live process holds it); the step then does nothing and retries after 1 s.
store.settleAbandoned(): the two housekeeping UPDATEs, called by the sweep only.
store.openSenders(): wa_id and count of due rows.

processor.kick(senders) appends one step per received message to the sender's lane; each step calls claimNext and runs what it gets. sweep() calls settleAbandoned, then appends steps for openSenders, all senders in parallel. src/app.ts:103 passes the senders, not the wamids. claimed_at then means 'work started'.

With turn ids given at commit, an undo reaches 'the newest change committed before it'. Today it reaches 'the newest batch whose message arrived before the asking message' (src/ledger.ts:189, i.id < cur.id). They differ only when a WhatsApp message and an MCP write overlap. Is commit order the one you want?

Should a failed message in between still close an open question, as today (the reader looks at the immediately preceding message, whatever its fate)? The proposal keeps that; the alternative is 'the previous turn', which would let a retried 'sí' answer.

During a deploy, when an older message of the sender is still held by the old process, do you prefer the newer message to wait (and possibly hit the 30 s deadline) or to be answered out of order? The claim redesign can do either; I would make it wait and retry after 1 s.
Should MCP writes show in the WhatsApp agent's conversation window? Today they do not; with the turn table it becomes a one-line choice.
After an outage the sweep sends one failure notice per message that passed its deadline, up to 50 in a pass (src/process.ts:511-515). Is one notice per message what you want, or one per sender?

verdict: redesign. The write path is careful: it checks the account, locks rows and refuses when something changed, and its tests drive behaviour through execute(), so they can prove a rewrite. Its weakness is identity, not correctness. A "batch" is a derived property of inbound_message (action and reply_text set, not an undo, at least one row in one of three tables) and is found by wa_id. Each of three stores records lineage its own way: movement points forward through superseded_by and backward through restores, fact is the same plus a DEFERRABLE nextval trick, and reminder only points backward. So undo needs three planners, a recursive walk, a 20-query loop and a special-cased four-way EXISTS. My answer to the council question has three parts. Yes to a channel-neutral `turn` table, locked per account, with MCP idempotency split into its own table. No to a separately written effect log: it would be the second source of truth that agent-spec.md:646-650 rightly rejected. Instead, give the three stores the same lineage columns (lineage_id, made_in, ended_in), define the effect log as a SQL VIEW over them, and write one undo engine with small per-entity hooks. Separately, applyCall is not the single write path it claims to be (reminders, forget-all and undo's internals bypass it). The execute/apply split is right in principle but drawn in the wrong place, and the outcome rendering is written twice, once per channel.

redesign.problem: inbound_message does four jobs. A batch is a derived predicate, `action IS NOT NULL AND reply_text IS NOT NULL AND undoes IS NULL` (src/ledger.ts:144-147). It is set by two writers in two modules, store.commit (src/store.ts:273-294) and settleBatchRow (src/ledger.ts:153-174), which sits in ledger.ts but writes inbound_message. Batches are found by wa_id (src/ledger.ts:189), which is why an MCP row has to carry wa_id, a fake wamid, `kind 'tool'` and `payload '{}'` (src/mcp/write.ts:31,124-125). MCP request ids are global, because wamid is UNIQUE across accounts (001_init.sql:6, src/mcp/write.ts:117), so one account's request_id blocks another's. The undo stack is ordered by inbound id, `i.id < cur.id` (src/ledger.ts:189). For WhatsApp that id is assigned at receipt, for MCP at request time, so a WhatsApp "deshacer" received just before an MCP write commits can miss that write (PLAUSIBLE, narrow window). The locks are three advisory keys taken in an order that depends on the path: undo takes 7203002, then movement rows, then 7203003, then 7203005 (src/undo.ts:86,95,97,100), while a WhatsApp turn [set_reminder, correct_movement] takes 7203005 and then a movement row in action order (src/execute.ts:268-273 then :129, src/apply.ts:181). A concurrent MCP undo and that WhatsApp turn can therefore deadlock (PLAUSIBLE; agent-spec.md:686-687 already records the movement-only variant as 'known, not fixed').

A turn row is inserted only at the commit point, in the commit transaction, so 'committed' means 'exists' and id order is commit order. WhatsApp: `inbound_message.turn_id bigint UNIQUE REFERENCES turn`. Transport, queue, send markers and pending question stay on inbound_message (that is another group). MCP: `mcp_request(account_id bigint, request_id text, call_hash text NOT NULL, result jsonb NOT NULL, turn_id bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES turn, created_at timestamptz DEFAULT now(), PRIMARY KEY (account_id, request_id))`, pruned after 24 h if wanted. Lock: every write turn (store.commit, writeAsMcp, the reminder CLI) starts with `SELECT 1 FROM account WHERE id = $1 FOR UPDATE`. That replaces advisory keys 7203002, 7203003 and 7203005 (src/undo.ts:86, src/facts.ts:70, src/reminders/db.ts:58) and removes every lock-order question. Row FOR UPDATE stays only where the reminder sweep competes (src/reminders/send.ts:163). Module: `src/turn.ts` exports `openTurn(tx, {accountId, channel, receivedAt}) → id`, `lastUndoable(tx, accountId, turnId)` and `markUndoes`. settleBatchRow and batchRow are deleted. Migration (016): create turn and `INSERT INTO turn (id, …) SELECT id, a.id, channel, received_at, updated_at, action, reply_text, undoes FROM inbound_message i JOIN account a USING (wa_id) WHERE action IS NOT NULL AND reply_text IS NOT NULL`, which keeps the ids so every existing FK value and every audit line such as 'undid batch 12' stays true. Then setval the sequence, set inbound_message.turn_id = id for channel='whatsapp', copy channel='mcp' rows into mcp_request (payload->>'input_hash', payload->'result'), and add one 'system' turn for reminder rows whose inbound_message_id IS NULL (src/reminders/cli.ts:91).

redesign.item: Uniform lineage columns + effect VIEW + one undo engine
redesign.problem: Each store records history differently. movement uses a forward superseded_by plus a backward restores, so followForward walks both directions (src/ledger.ts:259-275). fact uses a forward superseded_by with a nextval and DEFERRABLE dance (src/facts.ts:123-131, 011_facts.sql:24). reminder uses only a backward restores, so headOf loops up to 20 queries (src/undo-reminders.ts:32-43). 'What batch B did' is three hand-written classifiers: effectsOf (src/undo.ts:56-66), planFactUndo (src/undo-facts.ts:43-66) and planReminderUndo (src/undo-reminders.ts:53-76). The same net-of-nothing rules appear again in SQL in lastBatch (src/ledger.ts:192-204). Movements have no net-of-nothing rule at all: effectsOf checks deletedBy===batch first, so a row logged and deleted in the same batch would be 'restored' by undo. That is unreachable today, because the model never sees ids it just created (a latent asymmetry). The stale check needs settledBatches plus chain walks only because concurrent writers were not serialized (agent-spec.md:678-679: 'in ordinary use the stack makes this unreachable').
redesign.proposal: On movement, fact and reminder, add `lineage_id bigint NOT NULL` (the id of the first version), `made_in bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES turn`, `ended_in bigint REFERENCES turn` and `ended_at timestamptz` with CHECK ((ended_at IS NULL) = (ended_in IS NULL)), plus UNIQUE INDEX on (lineage_id) WHERE ended_in IS NULL, so the database enforces one live version per logical thing (today nothing enforces this for movements). Live is `ended_in IS NULL`, and for reminders also `AND next_due_at IS NOT NULL`. A correction ends the old row and inserts the new one with the same lineage. A delete, forget or cancel ends the row. A restore inserts a copy into the same lineage. The facts nextval/DEFERRABLE trick goes away because the old row is ended before the insert. Effect VIEW: `CREATE VIEW effect AS SELECT 'movement' entity, id, lineage_id, made_in turn_id, 'made' op FROM movement WHERE ended_in IS DISTINCT FROM made_in UNION ALL SELECT 'movement', id, lineage_id, ended_in, 'ended' FROM movement WHERE ended_in IS NOT NULL AND ended_in <> made_in UNION ALL …fact…reminder`. This one row-level rule is exactly the net-effect test: it covers the fact cases in src/ledger.ts:196-199 and the reminder case at :202-204, and it fixes the movement gap. lastUndoable becomes `…FROM turn t WHERE account_id=$a AND id<$cur AND undoes IS NULL AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM turn u WHERE u.undoes=t.id) AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM effect e WHERE e.turn_id=t.id) ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 1`. Engine (src/undo.ts, about 150 lines): for each lineage the turn touched, before = the version it ended that was made earlier, after = the version it made and did not end. 'As left' = the live head of the lineage has the same content as after (or there is no live head when after is null), checked under the account lock. This is the value comparison planFactUndo already uses (src/undo-facts.ts:54). Writes: end the head, and/or copy before into the lineage. Per-entity descriptor `{table, content: string[], restore?(tx, row, now) → 'ok' | 'stale'}`: movement has no hook; fact checks that its (kind, key) is free; reminder checks for a next occurrence and the MAX_REMINDERS cap and recomputes next_due_at. Identifiers go through postgres.js `sql(table)`. UndoOutcome becomes `{status:'undone', turn, items:{entity, did:'created'|'replaced'|'ended', before?, after?}[]} | {status:'nothing'|'expired'} | {status:'stale', items} | {status:'refused', entity}`, where the caller passes the entities it may undo: MCP passes movement and fact, which replaces the channel query at src/undo.ts:104-107. Migration (017, same release): backfill lineage_id with one recursive CTE from roots (rows no other row points to through superseded_by or restores) over the about 100 live rows. Set made_in = inbound_message_id. Set ended_in = COALESCE(deleted_by | forgotten_by | cancelled_by, the made_in of the successor). Keep the old columns for one release, with a test that the effect view's turns equal old lastBatch's on the test-harness fixtures, then drop superseded_by, deleted_*, forgotten_*, cancelled_*, restores and their indexes.

The layering "a write returns data, each channel presents it" is right and stays, but the batch is in the wrong place: it is an `inbound_message` row recognised by a latency label plus a reply text, owned through a phone-number string, and it forces a four-table EXISTS, fake MCP messages, three undo planners with three different definitions of "as the batch left it", and five lock keys taken in orders that can deadlock. My answer to the council question: yes to a channel-neutral `batch` table and one undo engine, no to a separate effect-log table. The three stores already are the effect log; give them the same three columns (`entity_id`, `created_in`, `ended_in`/`ended_at`) and one engine can read all of them, with no second source of truth to drift. `applyCall` is the single write path for six of the nine undoable writes only; make it cover all nine, give outcomes one status vocabulary, and render the record line in one place instead of two. Do it in three steps that each keep the suite and `pnpm eval:scenarios` green: (1) pure refactor of outcomes and record rendering, (2) `batch` table plus one account lock, (3) uniform version columns plus the single undo engine. redesign.item: 1. A `batch` table: where 'a batch of effects' lives, and its minimal definition
redesign.problem: A batch today is 'an inbound_message row with action and reply_text set that is not an undo' (src/ledger.ts:144-147). That makes a latency-report label load-bearing for undo, makes every non-writing message a candidate that a four-way EXISTS over movement, fact and reminder must filter out (src/ledger.ts:185-206), forces MCP to insert a fake message (`wamid 'mcp:<uuid>'`, `kind 'tool'`, `payload '{}'`, `status 'done'`, src/mcp/write.ts:123-127) and then roll it back by throwing `NothingChanged` when the call changed nothing (src/mcp/write.ts:83-88, 133, 155), and makes ledger.ts update `inbound_message` (src/ledger.ts:167-173) although store.ts claims that table. Ownership of a batch is a text match on `wa_id` (src/ledger.ts:188-189), not a foreign key to the account; `settledBatches` and `markUndone` take no account at all (src/ledger.ts:278-284, 318-320). Ledger rows also pin message rows forever through their foreign keys, so message bodies and payloads can never be pruned.
redesign.proposal:
Minimal definition: a batch is one committed request of one account that changed at least one stored row; it exists only if something was written. Tables:

CREATE TABLE batch (
  id bigint GENERATED BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  account_id bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES account (id),
  source text NOT NULL CHECK (source IN ('whatsapp','mcp','cli')),
  message_id bigint UNIQUE REFERENCES inbound_message (id),  -- the WhatsApp message, else null
  requested_at timestamptz NOT NULL,  -- the message's received_at, or now() for an MCP call: orders batches and bounds the 24 h window
  created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  undoes bigint UNIQUE REFERENCES batch (id) CHECK (undoes <> id));
CREATE INDEX batch_account_idx ON batch (account_id, id DESC);

CREATE TABLE mcp_request (
  account_id bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES account (id), request_id uuid NOT NULL,
  input_hash text NOT NULL, result jsonb NOT NULL, call jsonb, batch_id bigint REFERENCES batch (id),
  created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(), PRIMARY KEY (account_id, request_id));

Module src/batch.ts (about 80 lines, all SQL on `batch`):
  interface Write { tx; accountId; source; at: Date; messageId?: number; newest: number | null; batch(o?: { undoes: number }): Promise<number> }  // batch() inserts on first use, memoised
  writing(sql, o, fn: (w: Write) => Promise<T>): begins, locks the account (redesign 2), runs fn
  lastBatch(tx, accountId, before: Date): SELECT id, requested_at FROM batch b WHERE account_id = $1 AND undoes IS NULL AND requested_at < $2 AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM batch u WHERE u.undoes = b.id) ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 1
`requested_at < $2` keeps today's rule that an undo only reaches what was asked before it (`i.id < cur.id`, src/ledger.ts:189). A batch whose net effect is nothing (remember then forget the same new key in one message) now exists as a row: the undo loops to the next candidate when its plan is empty (bounded, e.g. 5).
MCP: under the account lock, look up `mcp_request` first, else apply, then insert the request row; no fake message, no exception as rollback. `mcp_request` can be pruned by age; `batch` never is.

Migration 016 from the live DB, ids preserved so no ledger row is rewritten:
  INSERT INTO batch (id, account_id, source, message_id, requested_at, created_at, undoes)
  SELECT i.id, a.id, i.channel, CASE WHEN i.channel = 'whatsapp' THEN i.id END, i.received_at, i.updated_at, i.undoes
  FROM inbound_message i JOIN account a ON a.wa_id = i.wa_id
  WHERE i.undoes IS NOT NULL OR i.channel = 'mcp' OR i.id IN (every inbound_message_id, deleted_by, forgotten_by, cancelled_by in movement, fact, reminder);
  then setval the identity to max(inbound_message.id); copy MCP rows into mcp_request (request_id = substr(wamid, 5)::uuid, hash and result from payload); drop and re-add the eight foreign keys to point at batch (id); delete the MCP rows from inbound_message; drop inbound_message.channel and inbound_message.undoes. One statement inserts all batches, so the self-reference on `undoes` is checked at statement end.

redesign.item: 2. One lock per account for every write transaction
redesign.problem: Three per-account advisory keys (7203002 undo, 7203003 facts, 7203005 reminders) plus movement row locks are taken in an order that depends on the order of the model's actions. That is a lock-order inversion between the two channels. Example by reading, not reproduced: a WhatsApp message whose actions are [remember_fact, correct_movement 5] takes the facts lock (src/facts.ts:142) and then the row lock on movement 5 (src/ledger.ts:85-88); a concurrent MCP `warren_undo_last` whose batch touched movement 5 takes the row lock first (src/undo.ts:95) and then the facts lock (src/undo-facts.ts:44). Postgres aborts one with 40P01; nothing retries, so a WhatsApp victim ends as 'commit failed' with the failure notice (src/process.ts:460). The same inversion exists between [set_reminder, remember_fact] (src/apply.ts:181 then src/facts.ts:142) and the undo (facts at src/undo.ts:97, reminders at :100). Per-sender ordering is an in-process promise chain for WhatsApp only (src/process.ts:534-555); MCP writes bypass it. src/concurrency.test.ts covers undo against a correction but has no case with a fact or reminder in the same message.
redesign.proposal: First statement of every write transaction (`writing()` in src/batch.ts): `SELECT id FROM account WHERE id = $1 FOR NO KEY UPDATE`. NO KEY UPDATE so that inserts holding FOR KEY SHARE on the account row through their foreign keys are not blocked. Order is then fixed: the message's own guard row (WhatsApp only, src/store.ts:276-279), then the account, then anything else. Delete `lockFacts`, `lockReminders`, the 7203002 lock and `lockRows`. Keep row-level FOR UPDATE only where a writer outside this lock exists: the reminder sweep (src/reminders/send.ts:153-163), which never takes the account lock, so no cycle is possible. With batch ids allocated under this lock, batch id order is commit order, which is what makes the single stale guard in redesign 3 a one-line comparison. Can ship before the batch table as a one-day change.

redesign.item: 3. The same three columns on movement, fact and reminder, and one undo engine (no separate effect-log table)
redesign.problem: What a batch did is already recorded on the rows, but each store spells it differently and links versions with pointers that must be walked: movement (`inbound_message_id`, `deleted_by`, `superseded_by`, `restores`), fact (`inbound_message_id`, `forgotten_by`, `superseded_by`, `restores`), reminder (`inbound_message_id`, `cancelled_by`, `restores`). Consequences: three planners (src/undo.ts 203 lines, src/undo-facts.ts 95, src/undo-reminders.ts 101) plus about 190 lines of undo SQL spread over src/ledger.ts:210-320, src/facts.ts:176-213 and src/reminders/db.ts:130-178; three different definitions of 'as the batch left it' (a chain walk with settled batches for movements at src/undo.ts:118-134, value equality for facts at src/undo-facts.ts:53-54, a restore-chain loop of up to 20 queries for reminders at src/undo-reminders.ts:32-45); a 50-hop recursive CTE (src/ledger.ts:259-275); a sequence value fetched ahead of the insert and a DEFERRABLE foreign key only so a fact can point forward at a row that does not exist yet (src/facts.ts:123-131, src/migrations/011_facts.sql:21); an UPDATE of `created_at` after insert that breaks the stated append-only rule (src/ledger.ts:118-120). Nothing in the database stops two live rows of one movement lineage. Five UPDATEs end or relink a row by id alone, with no account in the WHERE, although the docblock says every query takes the account (src/ledger.ts:121, 126, 312; src/facts.ts:158-159; src/reminders/db.ts:86-87 against src/apply.ts:84). They are safe today only because each caller did an account-scoped locked read first. The reminders slice shows the cost of the current shape: its undo was written by copying the facts one (docs/reminders-spec.md:106).
redesign.proposal:
Each store row is one version of an entity:
  entity_id bigint NOT NULL   -- the id of the entity's first version; copied to every later version
  created_in bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES batch (id)
  ended_in bigint REFERENCES batch (id), ended_at timestamptz
  CHECK (ended_in IS NULL OR ended_at IS NOT NULL)
  CREATE UNIQUE INDEX <t>_live_idx ON <t> (entity_id) WHERE ended_at IS NULL
Live is `ended_at IS NULL` on all three tables (one predicate, not three string constants). Log = insert. Correct = stamp the old version ended, insert a new version with the same entity_id (and the same `logged_at`, set in the INSERT). Delete, forget, cancel = stamp ended. A one-off reminder the sweep finishes gets `ended_at` with `ended_in` null. `superseded_by`, `restores`, `deleted_by`, `forgotten_by`, `cancelled_by` and their seven indexes go.

One engine, src/undo.ts, about 170 lines, generic over the table name (postgres.js `sql(table)` is the documented safe identifier helper):
  effects(tx, table, accountId, L): per entity touched by batch L, `before` = the version L ended that L did not create (or none), `after` = the last version L created that L did not end (or none).
  guard, same text for every store: stale if any version of the entity was created or ended by a batch X with X.id > L.id that is neither an undo nor undone; or if the entity's liveness now differs from what L left (catches the sweep and hand edits).
  invert: before none and a live version V: end V. before present and V live: end V, copy before. before present and nothing live: copy before. Both none: net of nothing, no item.
  `end` is one function for all stores: UPDATE t SET ended_at = now(), ended_in = $batch WHERE id = $id AND account_id = $account AND ended_at IS NULL RETURNING id (the account is in the WHERE, once).
  Per store only: `copy(w, fromId)` (the column list; reminders recompute next_due_at from `w.at` and may refuse: no occurrence left, cap), `rows(ids)` for rendering. About 25 lines each.
Items become { store, op: 'removed' | 'reverted' | 'restored', before?, after? } with typed rows; `renderUndo` keeps its wording.

Migration 017 from the live DB: add the columns nullable; `entity_id` by one recursive CTE from each root (a row with `restores` null that no row's `superseded_by` names) forward through `superseded_by` and `restores`; `ended_in`/`ended_at` from `deleted_by`/`deleted_at` (and the fact and reminder equivalents), and for superseded rows from the superseding row's `created_in` and that batch's `created_at`; finished one-offs get `ended_at = now()`; set NOT NULL, create the live index, drop the old columns. `created_in` is `inbound_message_id` renamed (ids were preserved in step 1). A handful of rows; verify with a query that live counts per account are unchanged before the drop.

Why not a separate effect table: it would restate what `created_in` and `ended_in` say, the sweep's and any manual change would not be in it, and rendering still needs the typed rows.
redesign.evidence: src/undo.ts:56-66 (effects rebuilt from pointer columns), :118-143 (chain guard); src/undo-facts.ts:42-66; src/undo-reminders.ts:32-45, 53-78; src/ledger.ts:210-315; src/facts.ts:123-131, 176-213; src/reminders/db.ts:130-178; the three LIVE constants at src/ledger.ts:31, src/facts.ts:27, src/reminders/db.ts:48. The movement stale guard is reachable only by an interleaving (cross-channel race, or a retried message committing after a later one) or by editing rows by hand: every test that reaches it writes `superseded_by` or `deleted_by` with raw SQL first (src/undo.test.ts:240-256, 257-268, 282-293). Reminders are not append-only: the sweep updates `next_due_at` and `sent_count` in place (src/reminders/send.ts:176, 180, 263; src/reminders/db.ts:200), which is why `copy` is the per-store hook.
redesign.size: About -590 lines of undo code across six files, +170 engine, +75 store hooks, +80 lines SQL: net about -350. Tests and fixtures reference the old columns roughly 150 times (counted with grep across src and evals: `superseded_by` about 60, `inbound_message_id` about 37, `deleted_by` about 24, `restores` about 17, the rest fact and reminder columns), mostly in seed helpers (src/command-fixtures.ts, src/mcp-test-kit.ts, evals/scenarios/drive.ts) and state assertions.
redesign.confidence: medium-high. The shape is sound and the live data is tiny; the risk is rewriting the highest-integrity code, so do it last and only with src/undo.test.ts, src/memory.test.ts, src/reminder-agent.test.ts, src/mcp-write.test.ts and the real-Postgres src/concurrency.test.ts passing unchanged in behaviour.

redesign.item: 4. One applyCall for all nine writes, one status vocabulary, one record renderer, one table of per-tool facts
redesign.problem: `applyCall` is documented as 'the one write path of both channels' (src/apply.ts:83-84) but covers six tools. Reminders have a second function with a second outcome union (src/apply.ts:156-206); 'forget everything' writes facts straight from execute.ts (src/execute.ts:231) and is an undoable batch effect; the undo writes through store functions directly. The reason given for the reminder split is that MCP does not expose reminders (src/apply.ts:154): the `WriteCall` type is doing double duty as the MCP allowlist. The Outcome union has no common status: `kind` is the status in six variants and the fact's kind (alias, category, note) in `remember_fact` (src/apply.ts:78), `undo_last` nests it in `undo.kind`, `remember_fact` in `stored.kind`, `forget_fact` has none and `gone` there means 'what was forgotten' while `kind: 'gone'` elsewhere means 'not found' (src/apply.ts:63, 75, 79-80). So both consumers re-derive status with if-ladders (src/execute.ts:138, 150, 158, 173-176, 193-201, 210; src/mcp/write.ts:199-345) and both render the same record line with the same arguments, each pre-reading `newestLiveId` for the `old.id === newest` flag (src/execute.ts:99, 135-213; src/mcp/write.ts:129, 199-345). Static facts about a tool are spread over the WriteCall union (src/apply.ts:26-37), a dead `WRITE_TOOLS` copy (:39-46), the case labels (src/execute.ts:122-127), `CHANGES` (src/execute.ts:77-87, compared against outcome strings at :350), `KIND_OF_TOOL` (src/agent/say.ts:95-105) and the 22-entry label map (src/action-label.ts:8-29). `CHANGES` and `KIND_OF_TOOL` are not compiler-checked: a new write tool left out of them fails silently (a voice transcript shown over a change record; a true 'anoté' dropped).
redesign.proposal:
Keep exhaustive switches for behaviour; remove the duplicated data.
(a) `WriteCall` = the nine tools that change undoable state: log_movements, correct_movement, delete_movement, undo_last, remember_fact, forget_fact, forget_all_confirmed, set_reminder, cancel_reminder. `applyCall(w: Write, call: WriteCall): Promise<Outcome>`; `applyReminderCall` and `ReminderOutcome` merge in. The MCP allowlist moves to src/mcp/write-tools.ts as `const MCP_WRITES = [...] as const satisfies readonly WriteCall['tool'][]`.
(b) Every outcome is { tool, status, ...data } with one `Status = 'applied' | 'unchanged' | 'gone' | 'full' | 'past' | 'nothing' | 'expired' | 'stale'`. A batch was made iff status is 'applied'. The fact's kind is named `factKind`; `forget_fact.gone` becomes `forgotten`.
(c) src/record.ts (pure, about 90 lines): `record(outcome, { today, newest }): { lines: string[]; detail?: string }`, the generalisation of `reminderReply`. execute.ts pushes its lines and `{ tool, outcome: status }`; mcp/write.ts takes `lines.join('\n')` as `record` and keeps only its structured view.
(d) One table next to the Action type: `ACTION_META = { log_movements: { label: 'log', claim: 'logged' }, ... } satisfies Record<Action['tool'], { label: string; claim?: keyof Applied }>`. `actionLabel`, `CHANGES` (tools with a `claim`) and `KIND_OF_TOOL` read it; src/action-label.ts is deleted. Leave src/agent/tools.ts alone: its order and bytes are the cached prompt prefix.
(e) `now` required in the context (today src/apply.ts:127 falls back to `new Date()` for MCP).
No schema change; this is step 1 and makes steps 2 and 3 smaller.
redesign.evidence: As cited in the problem, plus: `WRITE_TOOLS` has no reference outside its definition (grep over src and evals); the link and disconnect actions also write inside the commit transaction (src/execute.ts:236-267) but are not undoable and correctly stay outside applyCall; AGENTS.md documents `applyCall(tx, {accountId, inboundId, today}, call)` and docs/mcp-spec.md:92 `{accountId, requestId, today}` while the real context is `{accountId, batchId, position?, now?}` (src/apply.ts:48-57).
redesign.size: src/execute.ts 365 to about 240; src/mcp/write.ts 349 to about 240; src/action-label.ts -31; +90 src/record.ts; src/apply.ts about the same. Net about -150 lines.
redesign.confidence: high for (a), (b), (c), (e); medium for (d), which is tidiness more than risk reduction

redesign.item: 5. Split src/ledger.ts by what it owns
redesign.problem: AGENTS.md calls it 'All SQL on movement', but 468 lines hold four jobs: movement reads and writes (1-127), batch SQL that reads and writes `inbound_message`, `fact` and `reminder` (129-208, 277-284, 317-320), undo chain helpers (210-315), and find and summary queries (329-468). store.ts in turn claims `inbound_message` while ledger.ts updates it. Names collide inside the file: `BatchRow` is a movement row (211), `batchRow` an `inbound_message` predicate (144), `batchRows` a query (221), `settleBatchRow` makes a row a batch (153), `settledBatches` means undone-or-an-undo (278).
redesign.proposal: After steps 2 and 3 this mostly falls out: batch SQL lives in src/batch.ts, the undo helpers are gone, and what remains is src/movements.ts (versions: insert, lockLive, copy; about 110 lines) and the find and summary queries (about 140 lines, unchanged; they can stay in ledger.ts). While there: `supersede` becomes end-old plus one INSERT that sets `logged_at` (no follow-up UPDATE, no `id ?? null`); the word-splitting and LIKE-escaping lines duplicated at src/ledger.ts:355-358 and :401-404 become one helper.

Eleven result types for one idea: Outcome, ReminderOutcome, UndoOutcome, Undone, FactUndone, ReminderUndone, UndoLine, Remembered, Executed, Presented, Written. Target: Outcome (what a write did), UndoItem (one reverted entity), Executed (a WhatsApp turn), Written (an MCP answer).

challenged_decisions.challenge: Not a challenge to the goal, a challenge to its scope: for the write path the unit that must be serialised is the account, not the sender, because two channels write one account. The WhatsApp promise chain orders a sender's messages inside one process only; MCP writes do not pass through it, and the database-side locks that should cover the gap are taken in action-dependent order. I am saying explicitly that this is the only owner decision I push on, and only to widen it: keep per-sender ordering for the conversation, add one per-account lock for every write transaction.
challenged_decisions.evidence: src/process.ts:534-555 (in-process chain, 'Single process, so a promise chain is enough'); src/mcp/write.ts:121 (MCP opens its own transaction with no account lock); lock-order inversion between src/facts.ts:142 then src/ledger.ts:85-88 on one side and src/undo.ts:95 then src/undo-facts.ts:44 on the other. Read from the code, not reproduced.

challenged_decisions.decision: Undo within 24 h across channels (a WhatsApp 'deshacer' can undo an MCP write)
challenged_decisions.challenge: The decision holds and the redesign keeps it; I am flagging that the code already carves an exception in the other direction that the decision does not mention: an MCP undo refuses any batch that touched a reminder, and because undo always takes the newest batch, that one batch blocks MCP from undoing anything older until WhatsApp undoes it. Decide whether that is a rule (then make it a parameter at the MCP boundary) or a stopgap until MCP has reminder tools (then delete it).

questions_for_owner: Should an MCP client be able to undo a batch that set or cancelled a reminder once MCP has reminder tools (docs/reminders-spec.md:28)? If yes, `whatsapp_only` is deleted; if no, it becomes a `refuse` parameter passed by the MCP undo tool and the engine stays channel-free.

When a 'deshacer' is processed after a later message of the same person has already committed (a retry after a crash can do this: the sweep claims pending rows before a stale processing one), should it reach only what was asked before it (today's `i.id < cur.id`, which I kept as `requested_at < at`) or simply the newest committed batch? The first needs the stale guard to stay user-facing; the second would let the guard become an internal assertion.

A batch whose net effect is nothing (remember and forget the same new key in one message) is skipped silently today so 'deshacer' reaches the batch before it (src/ledger.ts:196-199). Keep that behaviour (the new engine loops past an empty plan), or answer that the last change left nothing to undo?

Is a fact that is remembered again after being forgotten the same fact (identity is account, kind and key) or a new one? It decides whether `fact.entity_id` is reused on re-remember, which lets the generic guard cover the 'said it again since' case with no fact-specific check.

Do you intend to prune or redact `inbound_message` bodies and payloads over time (privacy, more users)? If yes, that alone settles the batch-table question: today every ledger row holds a foreign key to a message row, so none can ever be deleted.

Does anything outside the repo (a manual SQL habit, a dashboard) read `movement.position` or the exact `inbound_message.action` labels? Inside the repo nothing but a test helper reads `position`, and only the latency report reads the labels.

verdict: adjust, leaning to a medium redesign of the history columns. The underlying model is right: versioned append-only rows, a batch as the unit of undo, all-or-nothing stale refusal, and stack semantics with no redo. Keep it. Do not move to event sourcing, and do not add a separate effect table. What is wrong is that the three stores spell one concept three ways. They use different "ended" columns (superseded_by/deleted_by, superseded_by/forgotten_by, cancelled_by), different `restores` semantics and different definitions of "as the batch left it". The cause is that no row has a stable entity identity. That forces a recursive chain walk for movements (ledger.ts:259-275), a 20-query loop for reminders (undo-reminders.ts:32-43), a value-equality check for facts (undo-facts.ts:53-54), and a four-way EXISTS that repeats each planner's "net of nothing" rule (ledger.ts:192-204 vs undo-facts.ts:48-51 and undo-reminders.ts:61). Give every versioned table the same five lineage columns (entity_id, made_by, ended_at, ended_by, copy_of), derive the effect log as a view, and write one ~140-line undo engine with per-store hooks only for reminders' real side effects. One account-row lock replaces three advisory keys. One SQL data migration with backfill gets there from the live DB. Do not reset it.

keep.item: Versioned append-only rows for movement, fact and reminder (a new row per change, a soft end, no DELETE)
keep.why: This is the right shape for a money ledger. Live totals are one partial-indexed filter (005_corrections.sql:16-19), and "antes …" comes from typed columns, not from jsonb. Event sourcing would add projections and replay with no consumer. Current rows plus an audit log would overwrite money rows (AGENTS.md rule 3) and push stale detection into jsonb comparison.

keep.item: Deriving a batch's effects from the rows themselves instead of a separate effect table (agent-spec.md:646-650)
keep.why: The original argument still holds: a separate effect table is a second source of truth that every write site must keep in step. With uniform lineage columns, a UNION ALL view gives the one effect log both briefs want, with nothing to drift. I keep this decision against both briefs' suggestion of an effect table.

keep.item: inbound_message_undoes_idx (unique undoes, 009_undo.sql:12) and the CHECK undoes <> id
keep.why: This is the database half of "a batch is undone once, whatever races". It carries over unchanged to whatever batch table the turn redesign produces.

keep.item: Stack semantics: the newest batch that is neither undone nor an undo, no redo (agent-spec.md:669-672)
keep.why: Simple and correct. It is also what makes most of today's stale machinery unnecessary (see the redesign items).

keep.item: All-or-nothing stale refusal, and the 24 h window computed in SQL from the batch's time (ledger.ts:186, undo.ts:89)
keep.why: Owner decision and correct. The engine keeps both.

redesign.item: Uniform lineage columns on movement, fact and reminder (migration 016_versions.sql)
redesign.problem: Each table invents its own lineage. movement uses superseded_by, deleted_at/deleted_by and restores (003/005/009). fact uses superseded_by DEFERRABLE, forgotten_at/forgotten_by and restores (011:28-31). reminder uses cancelled_at/cancelled_by and restores, with no supersede (014:24-26). No row has a stable entity identity, so finding where a movement or reminder stands now means walking pointers. Facts dodge this only because (kind, key) happens to be an identity. There is no database guarantee that a movement chain has at most one live row. 'Live' is three string constants spliced with sql.unsafe (ledger.ts:31, facts.ts:27, reminders/db.ts:49).
redesign.proposal:
Every versioned table gets the same columns, with no others for lineage:
- `entity_id bigint NOT NULL DEFAULT nextval('<table>_entity_seq')`: stable across versions. A new entity takes the default, and a new version passes its entity_id.
- `made_by bigint NOT NULL`: the batch that wrote this version. Renamed from inbound_message_id, and an FK to inbound_message until the turn/batch table lands.
- `ended_at timestamptz` and `ended_by bigint`, with `CHECK ((ended_at IS NULL) = (ended_by IS NULL))`.
- `copy_of bigint REFERENCES <table>(id)`: set only by an undo, to the origin version whose values it copies, `coalesce(src.copy_of, src.id)`.

redesign.proposal:
Views from migration 016:
```sql
CREATE VIEW version AS
  SELECT 'movement'::text AS store, id, account_id, entity_id, made_by, ended_by, copy_of FROM movement
  UNION ALL SELECT 'fact', id, account_id, entity_id, made_by, ended_by, copy_of FROM fact
  UNION ALL SELECT 'reminder', id, account_id, entity_id, made_by, ended_by, copy_of FROM reminder;
CREATE VIEW batch_effect AS
  SELECT b AS batch_id, store, account_id, entity_id,
    max(id) FILTER (WHERE ended_by = b AND made_by <> b) AS before_id,
    max(id) FILTER (WHERE made_by = b AND ended_by IS DISTINCT FROM b) AS after_id
  FROM version, LATERAL (VALUES (made_by), (ended_by)) t(b) WHERE b IS NOT NULL
  GROUP BY b, store, account_id, entity_id;
```
A row with both ids null is a net of nothing. before and after set is 'changed', before only is 'ended', after only is 'created'. One rule covers every store.

lastBatch becomes: the newest write batch of the account, not undone and not an undo, with `EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM batch_effect e WHERE e.batch_id = i.id AND (e.before_id IS NOT NULL OR e.after_id IS NOT NULL))`.

The stale check is O(1) and needs no walk. For each effect, read the live version `cur` of the entity FOR UPDATE. It is as the batch left it iff:
- after set: cur exists, `coalesce(cur.copy_of, cur.id) = coalesce(after.copy_of, after.id)`, and `store.stillLive(cur)` holds (reminders: next_due_at not null);
- after null: cur is null;
- and, if before is set, `store.canRestore(before, now)` holds (reminders: nextOccurrence, plus the cap counted once over the plan).

This is enough because of the stack. Any later batch that touched the entity is either undone or an undo, otherwise it would be lastBatch. So the only things that can move an entity are out-of-band edits, races and the reminder sweep, and every one of those yields a version whose origin differs or that is no longer live.

Apply: for each effect, end cur if there is one (`UPDATE t SET ended_at = now(), ended_by = $undo WHERE id = cur AND ended_at IS NULL`, generic through sql(table)). Then, if before is set, `store.copy(tx, before, undoBatch, now)`, an INSERT…SELECT with entity_id, copy_of = origin and logged_at. Reminders recompute next_due_at there. Ending before inserting means fact_live_key_idx never sees two live rows, so the deferral goes.

Interface:
```ts
interface VersionedStore { table: 'movement'|'fact'|'reminder'; stillLive?(row): boolean; canRestore?(tx, row, now): Promise<boolean>; copy(tx, o:{from:number; batch:number; position:number; now:Date}): Promise<number> }
undoLast(tx, {accountId, batchId, now, stores}): Promise<UndoOutcome>
type Undone = { store; op: 'created'|'changed'|'ended'; before: Row|null; after: Row|null; now: Row|null }
type UndoOutcome = {kind:'undone'; batch; items: Undone[]} | {kind:'nothing'} | {kind:'expired'} | {kind:'refused_store'; store} | {kind:'stale'; items: {store; row}[]}
```
The renderers map (store, op) to today's lines. Cross-channel undo is unchanged, because the batch is found by account, not channel. The 24 h window is unchanged.

verdict: redesign. All paths below are under /Users/ticianomorvan/Projects/personal/warren. The behaviour of this group is right and well tested (LIFO undo, all-or-nothing, 24 h, never a redo, at-most-once reminder sends), but the storage shape makes every store re-derive the same three things by hand: what a batch did, where an entity stands now, and who may write. redesign.proposal:
Two tables, written only inside the commit transaction.

CREATE TABLE batch (
  id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  account_id bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES account (id),
  turn_id bigint UNIQUE REFERENCES <turn or inbound_message> (id),  -- null for a CLI write; UNIQUE is the second layer of 'applied once'
  undoes bigint REFERENCES batch (id),
  created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  CHECK (undoes <> id));
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX batch_undoes_idx ON batch (undoes) WHERE undoes IS NOT NULL;
CREATE INDEX batch_account_idx ON batch (account_id, id DESC);

CREATE TABLE effect (
  id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  batch_id bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES batch (id),
  account_id bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES account (id),
  store text NOT NULL CHECK (store IN ('movement','fact','reminder')),
  entity_id bigint NOT NULL,
  before jsonb,          -- null: this effect created the row
  after jsonb NOT NULL); -- the row's person-set columns; a removal is removed_at inside the image
CREATE INDEX effect_batch_idx ON effect (batch_id, id);
CREATE INDEX effect_entity_idx ON effect (store, entity_id, id DESC);

Rules: the batch row is inserted lazily at the first effect, under the account lock, so a batch exists only if it changed something and batch ids are in commit order per account. Images are built in SQL by each store with an explicit `jsonb_build_object` and amounts as text (`amount::text`), and are applied back in SQL; the app never parses an amount out of one (rule 1). The row change and its effect go in one statement (a data-modifying CTE: `old` SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, `new` UPDATE ... RETURNING, INSERT INTO effect SELECT old.image, new.image), so they cannot drift. `lastBatch` becomes: newest batch of the account with `undoes IS NULL` and no batch that undoes it.

'Append-only' is a convention with exceptions already: `created_at` is updated (src/ledger.ts:118), and the sweep updates `next_due_at` and `sent_count` in place (src/reminders/send.ts:176, 180, 263; src/reminders/db.ts:200). The three stores differ in what they guard: `softDelete` and `supersede` have no live or account predicate and no row count (src/ledger.ts:121, 125-127), while `forgetFact` and `cancelReminder` check both live and row count (src/facts.ts:156-161, src/reminders/db.ts:84-89). Facts need a `nextval` plus deferred-FK dance to swap a version (src/facts.ts:123-131, src/migrations/011_facts.sql:21). Nothing in production reads the version chain except undo: 'antes ...' is rendered at write time from the in-memory old row (src/render.ts:199, 404).
redesign.proposal:
One row per entity, updated in place, never hard-deleted; history lives in `effect`.

movement(id, account_id, direction, amount, currency, occurred_on, description, category, payment, confidence, created_at, removed_at)
  indexes (account_id, id DESC) and (account_id, occurred_on), both WHERE removed_at IS NULL
fact(id, account_id, kind, key, value, created_at, removed_at)
  UNIQUE (account_id, kind, key) WHERE removed_at IS NULL
reminder(id, account_id, what, schedule, created_at, removed_at, next_due_at)   -- next_due_at is scheduler state, not in the image
reminder_send unchanged.

Dropped columns: `superseded_by` (2 tables), `restores` (3), `deleted_by`, `forgotten_by`, `cancelled_by`, `inbound_message_id` (3; provenance is first effect -> batch -> turn), `movement.position`, `reminder.sent_count`, and their 9 `*_by`/`restores` indexes. 'Live' is `removed_at IS NULL` everywhere, so the three `LIVE` string constants and about 20 `sql.unsafe(LIVE)` splices go (src/ledger.ts:31, src/facts.ts:27, src/reminders/db.ts:49). A correction is one UPDATE with the same id; a fact update is one UPDATE; undoing a delete clears `removed_at` on the same row. Every write statement carries `account_id` itself.

Why not the alternatives: event sourcing needs projections, replay and versioned event schemas for no consumer; versioned rows make every reader filter and every outside reference chase ids. A test-only invariant keeps the log honest: for every row, its image equals the `after` of its newest effect.

redesign.item: One per-account write lock
redesign.problem: Three advisory keys for one idea: 7203002 undo (src/undo.ts:86), 7203003 facts (src/facts.ts:70), 7203005 reminders (src/reminders/db.ts:58), plus row locks on movements (src/ledger.ts:80-89, 238-242) and a second live-lock pass on heads (src/undo.ts:139-144). The comment that lists the keys omits 7203005 (src/db.ts:19-20). The order differs by path: an undo takes movement rows, then facts, then reminders (src/undo.ts:95, 97, 100); a WhatsApp message takes them in the model's action order (src/execute.ts:110-133). A message that remembers a fact and then corrects movement X, running beside an MCP `warren_undo_last` whose batch holds X, is a lock cycle. MCP requests are outside the per-sender lane (src/process.ts:534-555), nothing retries 40P01, and the loser gets the failure notice (src/process.ts:459-460) or an MCP error. Narrow, but the spec's 'never one sender' (docs/agent-spec.md:685-686) stopped being true when MCP writes shipped.
redesign.proposal: `lockAccount(tx, accountId)` = `SELECT 1 FROM account WHERE id = $1 FOR NO KEY UPDATE`, the first statement of `store.commit` and `writeAsMcp`, before anything is read. `NO KEY` so that inserts with an `account_id` foreign key elsewhere (the webhook's message insert) do not wait on it. Every write for a person then runs one at a time, caps are decided under it, and batch ids are in commit order. Drop `lockFacts`, `lockReminders`, `lockRows`, `lockLive`, the undo advisory lock and the head re-check. Keep only the `FOR UPDATE` on a reminder row, for the sweep. Lock order is then account -> reminder row for people and reminder row alone for the sweep: no cycle. The commit transaction holds no model call (src/process.ts:432-458), so the lock is held for milliseconds.

redesign.item: Migration path from the live DB
redesign.problem: The new shape cannot be reached by additive columns alone: superseded movement and fact rows are old versions, not entities, and must leave the live tables.
redesign.proposal: One file, `016_history.sql`, run by the existing single-transaction migrator (src/db.ts:23-34), after a `pg_dump` of the live DB. Steps: (1) `CREATE TABLE movement_v1 AS TABLE movement`, same for `fact` and `reminder`: archives nothing reads. (2) Create `batch` and `effect`. (3) Backfill `batch` in id order from every `inbound_message` that is a batch today (`action` and `reply_text` set), with `turn_id` = its id, `undoes` mapped, `created_at = received_at`. (4) Drop the self-referencing foreign keys, delete superseded rows from `movement` and `fact`, rename `deleted_at`/`forgotten_at`/`cancelled_at` to `removed_at`, drop the pointer columns, `position`, `sent_count` and their indexes. Surviving rows keep their ids, so ids in recent replies and in `reminder_send` stay valid. (5) Insert one create-effect per surviving row, under the batch of the message that made it. (6) Drop `inbound_message.undoes`. What is lost: 'deshacer' for corrections and deletes made in the 24 h before the cutover (their before-images are only in the `_v1` archives). With one user, deploy after a quiet day or accept it. Proof, in src/migrations.test.ts, which already applies a migration over seeded rows: totals per direction and currency of live movements, the set of live facts and the set of live reminders with `next_due_at` are equal before and after, and every row's image equals its newest effect's `after`.

challenged_decisions.decision: AGENTS.md rule 3 as written ('Corrections never overwrite a movement, deletes never remove one, and neither does an undo'), and the slice C decision 'The action log is the data already stored; no table' (docs/agent-spec.md:645-650). I challenge the letter of both. I do not challenge the owner's listed decision: visible history ('antes ...') and undo within 24 h across channels are kept exactly.
challenged_decisions.challenge: Keep the intent (nothing is ever lost, every change is recorded append-only, an undo is itself recorded) and move the guarantee from three tables of version rows to one insert-only `effect` log, with entity rows updated in place under a stable id. If the owner holds the letter of rule 3, the same batch, effect log, engine and lock still apply: only the image format changes, from jsonb images to typed per-store history tables (three more tables, and readers keep filtering for the head row). That choice is the debatable part; the batch and the engine are not.
challenged_decisions.evidence: (1) Rows are already updated in place: `created_at` (src/ledger.ts:117-120), the ending stamps, and `next_due_at`/`sent_count` by the sweep (src/reminders/send.ts:176, 180, 263). (2) No production code reads the version chain except undo; 'antes' is rendered from memory at write time (src/render.ts:199, 404). (3) The 'no second source of truth' argument did not hold: batch-ness is encoded twice, in SQL and in TypeScript, and the mismatch jammed undo (docs/agent-spec.md:1166-1170). (4) Ids change on every correction (src/ledger.ts:111-122), which every future reference to a movement (a statement line, a budget, a pending question) would have to chase. (5) docs/mcp-spec.md:120-121 already states the batch table is what would be built from scratch. Costs I accept and name: jsonb images lose column types (mitigated by explicit images with amounts as text, applied in SQL, and a 24 h replay window), and an in-place UPDATE is one bug away from changing an amount, as it is today since nothing in the database forbids `UPDATE movement SET amount` now.

questions_for_owner: Is rule 3 about the rows (a movement row's values are never updated) or about the record (every change is kept, append-only, and shown)? The first means typed history tables per store; the second allows current rows plus one effect log, which is what I would build.

When a person says 'olvidate de ...', should the value be erased after the 24 h undo window? Today a forgotten fact keeps its value forever (src/facts.ts:156-161 only stamps). An effect log can prune fact images by age; version rows cannot easily.

Is it acceptable to lose 'deshacer' for corrections and deletes made in the 24 h before the migration, or should the migration backfill their before-images from the superseded rows (about 30 more lines of SQL)?

Which order defines 'the last thing' when channels overlap: commit order (my proposal, the batch id) or arrival order (today, `i.id < cur.id` at src/ledger.ts:189)? They differ only when an MCP write commits while a WhatsApp 'deshacer' is still in the model.

A batch that can never be undone blocks every older batch: after a one-off reminder was sent, each 'deshacer' answers stale and the café logged before it is out of reach (src/undo-reminders.ts:64, src/undo.ts:135-137). Keep the strict stack, or let the engine pass over a batch that is blocked for good?
Should MCP keep refusing to undo a batch that touched reminders once MCP has reminder tools? In the redesign it is one argument (`stores`), so it is a product choice, not a code one.

Do you want the database to refuse a movement write with no effect row (a trigger, or a test-only invariant query)? I would start with the single-statement writer plus the invariant in tests, and add a trigger only if a second writer path appears.
